entry.title: Ecco2K, Whait, Angelo LeRoi, and More: This Week’s Pitchfork Selects Playlist
entry.summary: Our weekly playlist highlights songs that our writers, editors, and contributors are listening to on repeat
entry.content:
The staff of Pitchfork listens to a lot of new music. A lot of it. On any given day our writers, editors, and contributors go through an imposing number of new releases, giving recommendations to each other and discovering new favorites along the way. Each Monday, with our Pitchfork Selects playlist, we’re sharing what our writers are playing obsessively and highlighting some of the Pitchfork staff’s favorite new music. The playlist is a grab-bag of tracks: Its only guiding principle is that these are the songs you’d gladly send to a friend.

entry.title: The Weeknd Debuts “Hong Kong” in Hong Kong
entry.summary: Faye Wong features on the new song, premiered during his four-night run at Kai Tak Stadium
entry.content:
Opening a four-night run at Kai Tak Stadium in Hong Kong, the Weeknd debuted the thematically apt “Hong Kong” on Saturday. The new song features the Hong Kong singer-songwriter and actor Faye Wong, who also stars in a sleek visual accompaniment, set in the nation’s capital. You can watch the performance below.

Earlier this year, the Weeknd premiered another metropolis-themed song, “Rio,” in the titular city (that one was a duet with Anitta, who previously joined Tesfaye on “São Paulo”) along with a track that sampled the theme from Neon Genesis Evangelion. His previous album, Hurry Up Tomorrow, came out last February.

entry.title: Throwing Muses Reissue Self-Titled Debut Album for 40th Anniversary
entry.summary: Throwing Muses introduced 4AD’s first American signing to the world
entry.content:
Rhode Island indie rock legends Throwing Muses will reissue their long-out-of-print (and off streaming) self-titled debut this December, in honor of its 40th anniversary. The new edition of Throwing Muses, due December 11 on 4AD, celebrates the first full-length album by the first American band ever signed by the label, a major inflection point in its history.

The quartet of of vocalist Kristin Hersh, guitarist-vocalist Tanya Donelly, bassist Leslie Langston, and drummer David Narcizo were still teenagers when they released Throwing Muses in 1986. The album largely drew inspiration from a car accident that left a 16-year-old Hersh, the band’s primary lyricist, with a rod in her skull. In the aftermath, she says she began hallucinating songs like the snarling tracks Throwing Muses would eventually release.

“I can’t even remember what it was like to hear a song that didn’t grab my face and shout at it,” Hersh wrote in her 2010 memoir Rat Girl. “Must’ve been soothing. But this is electrifying.”

After 4AD signed Throwing Muses, the label’s direction shifted towards American alternative rock, exemplified by their signing of the Pixies in 1987. Throwing Muses went on to release seven albums and two EPs on 4AD. Their most LP was 2025’s Moonlight Concessions. The group has also spawned multiple side projects, including 50FootWave and Lakuna.

Revisit Katherine St. Asaph’s Sunday Review of Throwing Muses.

entry.title: Elvis Presley Catalog Owners Sue AI Company Anthropic for Copyright Infringement
entry.summary: The lawsuit claims Anthropic illegally used 274 songs by The King to train its AI model Claude
entry.content:
The licensing group that owns the rights to Elvis Presley’s music and license has filed a $41 million lawsuit against AI company Anthropic. The Tennessee-based Authentic Brands Group alleges that Anthropic infringed on their copyright by training its AI model Claude on 274 of Presley’s songs without permission, including “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” “Don’t Be Cruel,” “Farther Along,” “If You Think I Don’t Need You,” and “Run On.”

The lawsuit, filed on October 23 and viewed by Pitchfork, seeks roughly $150,000 in damages per song, adding up to $41 million. Authentic Brands Group filed alongside a number of co-plaintiffs with ownership over Presley rights. “The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in a statement. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.” Pitchfork has reached out to representatives for Anthropic for comment.

Although major labels and music publishers have filed claims against Anthropic before, Authentic Brands Group’s lawsuit is one of the first high-profile cases wherein the owner of a single artist’s catalog sued for copyright infringement. The lawsuit claims that Anthropic has illegally used the aforementioned Presley songs to create “unlicensed derivative works” with Claude.

“Even after the Defendant supposedly put up ‘guardrails’ after being sued, in one of its latest iterations, Claude continues to infringe: when recently asked to recreate specific songs ‘for a modern audience,’ Claude did so and admitted: ‘These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges,” the lawsuit reads. “That’s edging past ‘inspired by’ into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out.’”

entry.title: Watch Jay-Z Bring Out Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg at LA Tour Closer
entry.summary: Too $hort, John Legend, Scarface, and Blue Ivy Carter also joined the final Jay-Z 30 shows at SoFi Stadium
entry.content:
Jay-Z closed out his Jay-Z 30 tour this weekend at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium, bringing an end to a headlining run that broke Yankee Stadium’s ticket sales record and featured guest appearances from Nas, The-Dream, Rihanna, and Beyoncé. The tour celebrated the 30th anniversary of Jay’s debut album Reasonable Doubt, and kicked off earlier this year with a headlining show at Philadelphia’s Roots Picnic.

On Friday, October 23, he invited Scarface to the stage to rap “This Can’t Be Life” and “Mind Playing Tricks on Me.” Following with prior tour stops, Jay’s daughter, Blue Ivy Carter, accompanied him on piano during “The Story of O.J.” and “Dead Presidents / Dead Presidents II.” After ending his main set with “Public Service Announcement,” he returned to the stage for an encore with two more guests: John Legend and DJ Khaled, who joined him in a performance of their eight-plus-minute song “God Did."

The second and final night of the tour saw Jay-Z joined by Too $hort for a medley of his well-known “Blow the Whistle Freestyle” and the original 2006 “Blow the Whistle.” But the marquee guest spot of the evening featured Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg, both of whom came out to perform a medley of hits including “The Next Episode,” “Still Dre,” “Nuthin But a G Thang,” and of course, “California Love.” Jay also took the opportunity to honor late Los Angeles rapper Nipsey Hussle, who was killed in a 2019 shooting. He projected a black-and-white photo of the artist while playing his song “Hussle & Motivate,“ then incorporated the rapper’s “Last Time That I Checc'd” into a performance of “On to the Next One.”

During the tour closer, Jay-Z also took a moment to address criticism of the tour, specifically around alleged low-priced resale tickets, circulating online. ”Y’all gotta be very aware of what’s going on in the world, right? People will tell you that nobody was in here tonight, but you got eyes, you can see. People will tell you that the music wasn’t great, but you got ears,” he said. “You gotta understand, you gotta question everything in this world of AI.”

entry.title: Turnstile Pack Out Washington Monument for Palestine, Sudan, and Lebanon Benefit Show
entry.summary: The Baltimore hardcore band raised over $220,000 for Human Concern International’s relief efforts in the three regions
entry.content:
Turnstile took over the National Lawn in Washington, D.C. on October 24 with a massive free show raising funds for Human Concern International’s relief efforts in Palestine, Sudan, and Lebanon. The benefit concert concluded Turnstile’s second North American tour in support of their Grammy-winning album Never Enough. Check out footage from the show—and a full set list—below.

Per the Baltimore Banner, the first two fans in line for the 3 p.m. show arrived at the National Lawn at 5:00 a.m. All told, the National Park Service estimated that around 60,000 people were in the crowd. Turnstile aimed to raise $150,000 for Human Concern International; as of this writing, the show’s official LaunchGood page has raised over $221,000.

At the middle of the set, frontman Brendan Yates thanked the crowd for showing out and supporting their cause, telling the crowd, “We’re so grateful to have been raised by this scene, one that taught us that music not only reflects the artist making it but the people and the world and the suffering and the joy that surrounds it.” He concluded by leading a chant: “Loud enough for the White House to hear it: Free Palestine! Free Sudan! Free Lebanon!”

The Washington Monument benefit show marked Turnstile’s biggest yet, but it’s not the first time they’ve played free of charge for a good cause. In 2025, the Baltimore band hosted a hometown show in Wyman Park Dell to raise money for the nonprofit Health Care for the Homeless, a Maryland nonprofit that provides medical care and housing assistance for people experiencing homelessness. They funded the production out of pocket, and the show raised over $35,000 for the organization.

The Saturday show only added to the list of milestones Turnstile has accomplished this year. In February, the band won their first two Grammy Awards, for Best Rock Album (for Never Enough) and Best Metal Performance (for “Birds”). They made history that night as the first band to earn nominations across the Rock, Metal, and Alternative music categories. In August, they released an album of Never Enough remixes, with features from Elton John, Panda Bear, Hayley Williams, Oklou, Slayyyter, Chanel Beads, and more. Just this month, they also made their Saturday Night Live debut, becoming the first hardcore group to play Studio 8H since 1981.

This year, however, has not been without its trials. In March, the band’s former guitarist Brady Ebert was arrested for attempted murder after allegedly hitting Yates’ father with his car. William Yates was hospitalized after suffering “severe physical trauma” to his legs in the alleged attack, the band said in a statement to Pitchfork. The band parted ways with Ebert in 2022, noting in their statement that this decision was made "in response to a consistent pattern of harmful behavior affecting himself, the band, and the community.” The statement concluded, ”We have no language left for Brady.”

Although Turnstile’s ’s Washington Monument show concluded the Never Enough tour, they already have a few forthcoming festival dates lined up. They’ll play Tyler, the Creator’s Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival in November, and have also been confirmed to Primavera Sound’s 2027 bill.

Learn all about Turnstile’s rise in Lawrence Burney’s cover story Turnstile Blew Up. Now What?

entry.title: Slayyyter Cancels Remaining UK and European Tour Dates
entry.summary: Laryngitis and vocal cord tears are forcing the singer “to go on medication and full vocal rest for at least two weeks”
entry.content:
Slayyyter is calling off the last shows of her ongoing UK and European tour on doctor's orders. In an Instagram story viewed by Pitchfork, the pop singer wrote, “I am heartbroken to share after multiple doctor visits i have laryngitis and vocal cord tears,” adding, “Because of this, i am forced to cancel the remaining UK/EU dates to avoid permanent damage to my voice.” Among the scrapped Wor$t Girl in America tour stops are Copenhagen, Hamburg, Warsaw, Prague, Berlin, Antwerp, Manchester, Birmingham, Glasgow, Brighton, and London. Slayyyter has promised full refunds to fans and is “already working on rebooking shows for next year.” You can read her full note below.

Speaking of next year, Slayyyter is still slated to play dates in 2027 across Australia, New Zealand, and South America. Before that, she’ll debut her Wor$t Girl companion album, Wor$t Man in America, on December 4.

Slayyyter:

hey guys, i am heartbroken to share after multiple doctor visits i have laryngitis and vocal cord tears and have been ordered to go on medication and full vocal rest for at least two weeks. Because of this, i am forced to cancel the remaining UK/EU dates to avoid permanent damage to my voice. full refunds will be available at point of sale.

my team and i are already working on rebooking shows for next year and i hope to have news to share very soon to make it up to you. I know how much time and effort is spent to come out to a show. some of you have traveled, some of you have made costumes, and i am completely devastated to not be able to give you the shows you were planning for. we are working hard to figure out a time to return so i can deliver an even bigger and better show for you all. i hope you know i will make this up to you . lots of love to you all. thank you for making this tour so spcial.”

entry.title: Noel Gallagher Talks Vegans, Macca, Underwear on Chicken Shop Date
entry.summary: “Do you know what’s not a high-flying bird? A chicken.”
entry.content:
“Do you know what’s not a high-flying bird? A chicken.” Noel Gallagher is the latest guest on Amelia Dimoldenberg’s Chicken Shop Date. In the new episode, the elder Gallagher brother opines on vegetarians (“Fuck those guys”), Macca (“He’s one of those rare people that when you meet him, you walk away from it feeling good about yourself”), and the long-standing rumor—started by him, mind you—that he doesn’t wear underwear onstage: “That’s nonsense—I wear two pairs of underpants.”

Throughout the clip, Dimoldenberg peppers Gallagher with her characteristically acerbic questions. Asked “how do you make a comeback feel natural and not desperate,” he replies, “You can’t make sure, you just gotta hope that you can do whatever it is you’re trying to do as well as you once did it. And in the case of Oasis, it became apparent after maybe a week in rehearsals that it was gonna be as good—if not better—than it ever was.”

At another point, Gallagher addresses that inscrutable “Champagne Supernova” lyric: “I mean, I’ve still no idea what ‘slowly walking down the hall/Faster than a cannonball’ means. Do you?” “Well, it means you’re walking quite fast,” Dimoldenberg replies, to which Gallagher counters, “I think it’s a drug reference.” The two also engage in some light football banter (Gallagher famously supports Man City, while Dimoldenberg is a United fan). Watch the full segment below.

After a 12-year run, Chicken Shop Date is winding down with its final season. Role Model and Jorja Smith have also made recent appearances on the show. Meanwhile, the second coming of Oasis will proceed apace well into 2027, with live dates across Europe, the UK, and the U.S. slated through September. Next month the band will be honored at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony.

Revisit Jazz Monroe’s live review of Oasis’ 2025 tour.

entry.title: Chappell Roan Duets With Caroline Polachek, PinkPantheress, and Lola Young
entry.summary: All on the closing night of Roan’s Los Angeles pop extravaganza, the Super Graphic Spectacular
entry.content:
Midwest Princess Chappell Roan anointed a dynasty of fellow royals to close out her two-night benefit concert in Los Angeles last night. Held at Shrine Auditorium, the Super Graphic Spectacular celebrated the first anniversary of Roan’s Midwest Princess Project, which supports young people from LGBTQ+ communities. After joining Caroline Polachek to do “Look at Me Now,” Roan stepped up for a headline set with surprise guests PinkPantheress (doing “Tonight”) and Lola Young (“Picture You”).

On Wednesday night, Roan’s first headline set of the extravaganza featured a surprise appearance from Christina Aguilera. For good measure, Roan also joined Charli XCX for “Boom Clap” at Kia Forum last weekend.

entry.title: 10 New Albums You Should Listen to Now: Alchemical Sisters, Fine, Shabazz Palaces, and More
entry.summary: Stream new releases from Alchemical Sisters, Fine, Shabazz Palaces, and Josh Johnson
entry.content:
With so much good music being released all the time, it can be hard to determine what to listen to first. Every week, Pitchfork offers a run-down of significant new releases available on streaming services. This week’s batch includes new albums from Alchemical Sisters, Fine, Shabazz Palaces, and more. Subscribe to Pitchfork’s New Music Friday newsletter to get our recommendations in your inbox every week. (All releases featured here are independently selected by our editors. When you buy something through our affiliate links, however, Pitchfork earns an affiliate commission.)

Alchemical Sisters: Alchemical Sisters [Interdimensional Transitions]

Octo Octa and Eris Drew’s B2B sets are the stuff of legend, but the married DJs had never collaborated on a record until they teamed up to remix Special Interest’s “Disco III” in 2021. For a joint moniker they chose “Alchemical Sisters,” a play, of course, on the Chemical Brothers. Nominative determinism at work: ’90s big beat—from Orb to Orbit—makes up the core DNA of their first full-length album as a duo. Pieced together in their New Hampshire log cabin, Alchemical Sisters is, writes Andrew Ryce in Pitchfork’s new review, “a four-dimensional record where the past endlessly loops back on itself,” where “originality and reference become one and the same.”

Fine: Jazz Dreams [Escho]

So insular is Fine Glindvad Jensen’s musical realm that one ends up reaching for increasingly tortured anachronisms just to map its periphery: Lana if she fronted the Warm Inventions, Hope Sandoval if she made Honeymoon, a Bond girl who’s also Julee Cruise. That’s not to say Jazz Dreams is unwelcoming; the second solo album from the Copenhagen artist known mononymously as Fine is plush, cozy even, steeped in paisley folk and jangle pop. But spend enough time in this incense-scented, velvet-upholstered lounge, and you may begin to see strange shadows crawling up the walls.

Ryan Hemsworth: Numbskull [Topshelf]

Longtime producer for the indie rock stars Ryan Hemsworth returns with his first solo album in nearly a decade to remind us what his own songwriting sounds like free from others’ ideas. Turns out, it’s caustic electropop, filtered through grainy fuzz, pop vocal hooks that could scale a mountain, and the type of slamming bass notes that could work just as well in EDM or synthpunk. Hemsworth doesn’t have anything to prove, though, which allows him to tap a few guest features—Tegan and Sara, Illuminati Hotties, MSPAINT, Allie—that showcase just how far a singer-songwriter’s ideas can extend in their own voice and beyond. It’s a mature choice, showcasing not just his own skills, but how strongly they lift friends around him, too.

Shabazz Palaces: It’s a Style Sport [Sub Pop]

On It’s a Style Sport, his first full-length in six years as Shabazz Palaces, Ishmael Butler slips back into the many guises of his multifarious rap project. Lead single “Ahh World (I Won The Alpha Bet)” sets lucid social commentary to ominous beats that sound like the very dystopian future he rallies listeners to prevent; “Jheri Curl Jump,” meanwhile, is a loquacious love story murmured over jittery electro-funk. Butler’s latest for Sub Pop follows the sibling mini-albums Exotic Birds of Prey and Robed in Rareness. The LP features, among others, Thaddillac, Evan Flory-Barnes, and Kassa Overall, pairing Butler’s own production with that of sometime Shabazz collaborator Erik Blood.

Josh Johnson: Animative [International Anthem/Nonesuch]

To say Josh Johnson has a lot going on would be an understatement. The Los Angeles composer and multi-instrumentalist—sax, keys, synth, and effects, if you're wondering—has released killer albums with his trio SML and Jeff Parker’s ETA IVtet, plus produced for Flea and Meshell Ndegeocello. Now he’s making his solo debut on International Anthem with a set of tracks that canonizes his pivotal role in the West Coast’s burgeoning experimental jazz revival. Per press materials, Johnson drew inspiration from his former teacher Wayne Shorter, the West African philosopher Malidoma Somé’s writings, and “non-Western ways of thinking about time and being.”

Caroline Rose: Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall [Suck]

Caroline Rose loves a good character. The New York singer-songwriter’s taste for writing people “who are a little strange, who are outsiders, who seem to fuck up a lot,” per a recent statement, fits nicely with their taste for genre-hopping. (To their credit, Rose hopped on the “concept album about fame” train years before it got cool again.) Their new album Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall, got them in the studio with the Paper Chase’s John Congleton, leaning into the breezy hooks and angsty energy of surf rock to translate personal encounters with the uglier corners of the Americana dream.

Brakence: Marrow [Columbia]

Brakence knew what he was doing when he titled his comeback single after four years of radio silence “Ready or Not.” Despite his extended absence (or maybe, in fact, because of it), the singer-songwriter-producer has held on to a fervent fanbase happy to keep running back Hypochondriac and supplementing with Quadeca and/or Jane Remover shows until he resurfaces. But he still has his own long shadow to stand up to, a challenge he meets with a hefty 18 new tracks that return to his glitch-crooner roots.

Sour Widows: Sigil [Julia’s War]

Bay Area duo Sour Widows drew inspiration for their latest from a pretty bleak source: an apocalyptic dream cofounder Maia Sinaiko had wherein “all traces of human civilization would soon be obliterated, our collective efforts lost forever; no one would ever know.” Sinaiko and bandmate Susanna Thomson lay out this premise in appropriately bleak tones of grunge, emo, and alt-rock. But working with Jay Som and Boygenius producer Melina Duterte, they also manage to infuse these heavy compositions with a sense of urgency, fleet-footedness, and, perhaps most importantly, hope.

Loidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers [Incienso]

After a 15-year career heavy with touring, it’s understandable that Loidis wants some peace. Lucky for us, that means continuing to make his special blend of minimal techno, ambient, and dub, as exemplified on the stellar 2024 album One Day. His next LP, From The Toolkit Of Lovers, was recorded in the summer 2025 and centers on drawn-out tracks with plenty of room for stretched-out builds and spacious transitions. In his own words, it’s ”a 110-minute meditation on life, love and dub.”

William Basinski: Passing the Cup of Sorrows [Temporary Residence Ltd.]

In the niche field of past-life regression therapy, “passing the cup of sorrows” describes a concept wherein two souls in the spirit world exchange energy, allowing one spirit to understand and forgive one who hurt them in a past life. These moments of spectral interplay inspired the avant-garde composer William Basinski’s first album in six years, a 40-minute suite of single-note piano and whispering electronics. He composed the piece almost entirely while watching testimonials of the therapy, using their relationship to fragmented and painful memories to guide his hand, mind, and heart.

entry.title: Ryan Gosling’s Band Dead Man’s Bones Tease Return
entry.summary: Gosling’s duo with Zach Shields appears to be preparing its first music in 17 years
entry.content:
Dead Man’s Bones, the spectral rock duo of Ryan Gosling and screenwriter Zach Shields, are planning a comeback 17 years after their first and only album. Eva Mendes, Gosling’s wife, started teasing the return yesterday in a post designed to “summon new music from DEAD MAN’S BONES.” She followed it with two spooky visuals—one cross-posted with the new Dead Man’s Bones Instagram page—in which a voice ominously intones a spell to conjure the project for a twilight dance on October 27.

The original Dead Man’s Bones album was a 2009 collaboration with the Silverlake Conservatory Children’s Choir, a California education organization founded by Flea. The duo has lain dormant since its promotional run behind that LP, though one of its songs, “Pa Pa Power,” found its way onto Cat Power’s 2022 album Covers.

entry.title: Raye Wins 2026 Mercury Prize
entry.summary: She beat out Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean, Jade, Nia Archives, and more
entry.content:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her second album This Music May Contain Hope. She clinched the award over competition including Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean, Florence and the Machine, Jade, and Nia Archives. It’s Raye’s first time winning the prize: her 2023 album My 21st Century Blues also made the shortlist, but lost out to Ezra Collective.

Accepting the award during a ceremony in Newcastle, Raye said: "Albums are so important, and not to be bitter–because I feel like I’m mostly at peace with my past–but to come from a place where it’s all about singles and chasing the next thing, I just feel so grateful to be recognised. Hope is a very cheesy word, especially for us British people, we don’t do that deep stuff like that, but hope is something we all need…so I hope that message comes across to anyone who needs it.”

Elsewhere in the ceremony, Raye performed This Music May Contain Hope’s "I Hate The Way I Look Today” accompanied by a full big band. A number of other nominees also took the staege: Jade performed “Angel of My Dreams” from That’s Showbiz, Baby, Dean sang "Let Alone The One You Love," and Florence and the Machine offered a rendition of “One Of the Greats.” Pulp also took the stage to play "Begging for Change" off the War Child Records compilation Help (2), which raised money for children living in war zones.

entry.title: Charli XCX Will Appear in a Martin Scorsese Film
entry.summary: She reportedly makes a cameo in What Happens At Night with Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence
entry.content:
When Charli XCX revealed the cover for Music, Fashion, Film, it boasted three heavyweights from each discipline: John Cale, Marc Jacobs, and Martin Scorsese. Now, the pop star and the director have reunited for Scorsese’s next movie, What Happens at Night. Variety reports that the psychological thriller, which stars Jennifer Lawrence and Leonardo DiCaprio as a married couple who travel to European small town to adopt a baby, will feature a cameo from Charli. The project, a co-production between Apple and StudioCanal, does not yet have a release date.

Despite asking on the MFF track “Camera” if it’s “fuckin’ stupid if I try to be a girl on the screen when I'm turning thirty-four,” Charli has had a major year on the big screen. She appeared in multiple movies last year, including Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex, Pete Ohs’ Erupja, and Aidan Zamiri’s mockumentary about Charli’s “BRAT era,” The Moment. She also wrote the soundtrack for Emerald Fennell‘s Wuthering Heights (which featured her first collaboration with Cale, “House”) and co-wrote music for A24’s Mother Mary.

Read Anna Gaca on Wuthering Heights and Harry Tafoya on Wuthering Heights: The Album.

entry.title: Westside Gunn Announces New Album Heelmatic
entry.summary: Lead single “Zilla” features rapping on a camel in front of the Great Pyramid
entry.content:
Wrestling fanatic/Buffalo ad-lib king Westside Gunn is back with a new album called, naturally, Heelmatic. It arrives with a video of lead single “Zilla,” which was shot on location in Egypt. The clip technically premiered on Instagram back in August, but we’re showcasing it here since it just hit YouTube. Behold as Gunn rides a camel in Cairo then in front of the Great Pyramid while he raps about Oakleys, Glocks, and “choppin' bricks karate type.”

“ALBUM OTW AND ITS ALL GRIMEY, DUSTY, SOULFUL, JAZZ INSPIRED mixed with FLYEST SHIT U EVER HEARD IN YA LIFE,” he wrote in a post teasing the album this summer. Heelmatic is out November 13 on Griselda Records/Mass Appeal.

Westside Gunn will be heading overseas shortly after the album’s release, for his Heel the World Tour 2: “Still Healing” trek. Those dates, across the UK and Europe, can be found below, along with the Heelmatic tracklist and album artwork. Gunn’s last full-length releases were a trio of 2025 mixtapes: 12, Heels Have Eyes 2, and Heels Have Eyes 3.

entry.title: The Strokes and Phoebe Bridgers to Play SNL
entry.summary: Oh and also Gracie Abrams
entry.content:
Saturday Night Live has revealed the musical guests for its first November episodes. The Strokes will return to the Studio 8H stage on November 6 opposite first-time host Druski. The following week, Phoebe Bridgers will give her first solo SNL performance (Boygenius were musical guests in 2023) since the great guitar smashing fiasco of 2021, on a John Mulaney-hosted episode.

SNL’s 52nd season has already featured performances from Rosalía, Turnstile, and Katseye. Taylor Swift also made a surprise appearance during the October 3 episode to present that week’s host, Dakota Johnson, with a birthday cake. After taking the weekend off, SNL will return on Halloween with Obsession’s Inde Navarrette hosting and Gracie Abrams performing.

entry.title: Kacey Musgraves Reveals Middle of Nowhere Companion Album
entry.summary: She’ll unvault the 16-track Tex Mex Tapes on January 15
entry.content:
With little warning, Kacey Musgraves has revealed the existence of an entire companion album to her new LP Middle of Nowhere. Billed as Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes, the 16-track release consists of 11 new songs and 5 covers, including a Spanish rendition of “Uncertain, TX” from the original record. It’s out January 15 via Lost Highway. Tonight, Musgraves will share “Weekend in Texas” and her version of the norteño standard “Mi Tesoro.” For now, check out the cover art and tracklist below.

Middle of Nowhere was led by the single “Dry Spell” and its title track. Since its May release, Musgraves has also shared a video for “Mexico Honey.” She’s currently winding down her North American tour in support of the album, which wraps up with two shows at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle on October 26 and 27.
